transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Petra 3 FP, Anselm 3 FP, Caddock 3 FP, Yarrow 3 FP. Face-up: The Hive Blight [H-02], Order of the Dry Saint [F-02].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain hammers the cedar-shingle roofs of Hollowmoot as you shelter under the eaves of the tollhouse, the whole town lit orange by warden torches guttering against the wet. A woman claws through the crowd toward you — soaked to the bone, barefoot, a rope of prayer-knots wound white-knuckled around one fist. She knows Petra's bell-coat, knows Caddock's midwife satchel, knows enough to beg rather than ask: her son Tomas followed the swarm-song three nights running, and last night he didn't come back. He was seen wading toward Saint Orrin's Drowned Temple. Behind her, two Causeway Wardens watch with crossed arms and torches low, already deciding whether this is a rescue or a house to burn.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Your boy will come home—I've sworn it. Sergeant, we go after him, not burn anyone.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra moves forward between the wardens and the soaked mother, putting herself squarely in the space between them. She locks eyes with Warden Sergeant Coyl, her bell-coat marking her role as she speaks with the weight of her oath behind every word.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The Drowned Temple — did Tomas speak of why he was drawn there? Did he say anything before he left?

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps forward slightly from the shelter of the eaves, water running off his coat. His eyes track the prayer-knots in the woman's fist, then the wardens behind her, then the soaked fabric clinging to her arms.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I deliver babies in swamp and storm both—I won't stand by while Wardens threaten to burn another house. When did you last see your boy, mother? What's his name?

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock steps into the rain, leaving the shelter of the eaves. She faces the Soaked Mother directly but doesn't flinch from the Wardens' watching eyes. Her hand moves to her midwife's satchel with the practiced motion of someone accustomed to working in any condition—ready.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I was guard here before my name went bad. This isn't about burning—not yet. Tell me about your son, and tell me true: when the swarm-song called, did he follow it willingly, or is something else wearing his skin now?"

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steps forward from the eaves into the rain, his militia-trained bearing settling over him like an old coat that still fits. He positions himself between the soaked mother and the Wardens in one steady motion, his weathered frame a quiet barrier between crisis and cruelty. The prayer-knots on her wrist catch his eye—he knows that knot-work, knows what fear looks like when it's wound tight enough to hurt.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: You're right to question me, Sergeant. My name earned its stain fair and square. But a boy's life isn't your moment to settle accounts with me—it's mine to try and make something better of.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Rapport: dice + - - -, invoking Vowed to Ring Everyone Home Before the Flood [PE-A2], Bell-Ringer's Apprentice Who Hears the Swarm-Song [PE-HC] → Superb (+5) vs Good (+3): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Coyl's jaw works, but he lowers his torch a fraction. "Go, then," he mutters, "but the gate seals at moonrise, and if that boy comes out hive-touched, I burn the house myself." The mother presses the prayer-knots into Caddock's hand — Tomas, nine years old, followed the swarm-song three nights running. Yarrow, Coyl's eyes linger on you a beat too long, an old debt unspoken. The four of you turn toward the black water and the drowned bells beyond.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The rain thins to a grey drizzle as your boat noses between broken pillars, the temple's flooded nave stretching ahead like a drowned cathedral of black water and sunken pews. Somewhere above, faint and wrong, a humming drifts down from the belltower — not quite words, not quite song. A robed figure steps out onto a half-submerged step, lantern raised, staff braced against the current: one of the Dry Saint's last sentinels, watching the water for exactly the kind of trespass you're about to commit. Behind him, water drips from the bell-ropes far above, and every sound you make rolls back to you twice, three times, swallowed slow by stone and flood. Tomas is up there somewhere, if he's still himself at all.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I hear him in the song, Brother. That's Tomas in the bell tower. I'm ringing him home—and you know that's my vow, flood or no flood.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps forward with quiet determination, her bell-coat marking her authority. Her eyes move past Brother Ilse toward the stairs that spiral up into darkness, following the source of the humming. She doesn't rush, but she doesn't stop either.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: That's not swarm-song. Not quite.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm leans forward in the boat, eyes fixed on the sentinel and the dark water. He listens intently to the humming drifting down from the belltower—trying to parse it, to hear whether there's intent or merely the mindless chorus of the hive.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: The boy is up there—Tomas. I know what the swarm-song does, Brother. I'm going up to help him.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock continues poling the boat toward the step without slowing. She grips the pole with weathered hands, the prayer-knots from Tomas's mother wound tight around her wrist. She keeps her dark eyes fixed on Brother Ilse as the boat slides closer through the flooded nave.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Brother Ilse—I'm Yarrow, militia guard from Hollowmoot. We've come for Tomas, a boy who followed the swarm-song. If the Order has cure lore, if he can be saved, we need to reach him before the blight marks him completely.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow guides the boat forward with steady, measured strokes, hands visible and calm. His eyes take in the Brother's posture, the dripping bell-ropes above, the water's cold breath against stone. He's held lines before—militia holds, weir-holds, promises made in anger—and he recognizes the weight of a threshold when he sees one. He meets Brother Ilse's lantern-gaze without flinching, but there's no aggression in him, only the hard clarity of a man who knows what needs doing.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: No—no, I hear it—that's my— no.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The swarm-song shapes itself around Petra's name and she stops dead, oar forgotten, eyes fixed on the dark stairwell — for one long breath she is not here at all. Brother Ilse sees it happen and plants his staff crosswise before the step. "The song has already got a hook in her," he says, not unkindly. "I cannot in good conscience let the Order's threshold be crossed by one already claimed." Anselm presses closer, straining to hear the shape beneath the hum — not mindless, he's almost sure, something with intent laced through it — while Caddock and Yarrow keep the boat steady against the current, Caddock's knuckles white around Tomas's mother's prayer-knots. Ilse's lantern doesn't waver, but his sandaled feet shift on the slick step, a man holding a line he's not sure he believes in anymore.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Brother, I hear the song calling my name. But I'm still here. And I'm going up to ring Tomas home.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra forces herself free from the paralysis with visible effort, her body tensing against the song's pull. She steps forward in the boat with the quiet authority of someone trained all her life to hear the swarm-song and ring the bells anyway. She meets Brother Ilse's eyes—not with defiance, but with absolute certainty.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: There's a child in there. Not the swarm-song—a boy's mind, but something enormous singing through him.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm leans forward in the boat, one hand braced against the rail, his gaze tracking the darkness of the spiral staircase. He listens with complete attention, trying to parse the layers of sound beneath the hum.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: That boy's up there and I'm getting him, Brother. Step aside.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock plants her pole deep and drives the boat forward without hesitation. Her weathered hands are white-knuckled around the wood, the prayer-knots wound so tight around her wrist they cut into her skin. She keeps her dark eyes fixed on Brother Ilse as she comes toward the step—steady, relentless, the way she's always pushed through flooded labors that wouldn't wait.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Brother, I held lines like yours when the flood came—I know what that doubt costs. But that boy's still singing for help, not drawing others into the swarm. Let us reach him.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steadies the boat against the current and meets Brother Ilse's wavering gaze directly. His hands are calm and visible, his posture steady—not challenging the threshold, but speaking to it as one line-holder to another, one who understands the impossible weight of choosing between doctrine and mercy.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Rapport: dice - 0 - -, invoking Vowed to Ring Everyone Home Before the Flood [PE-A2], Bell-Ringer's Apprentice Who Hears the Swarm-Song [PE-HC] → Great (+4) vs Great (+4): TIE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Brother Ilse steps aside for Petra, but the swarm-song surges the instant she crosses the threshold, coiling tighter around her name — a cold thread she can feel humming just under her skin now, impossible to fully shake.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Brother Ilse's staff scrapes back against stone as he yields the step, lantern light trembling on the black water. Caddock drives the boat past him with a single powerful stroke, the hull sliding through the gap he leaves — clean, sure, no wasted motion, prayer-knots biting red lines into her wrist. Petra crosses the threshold on her heels, and the instant her boots touch the wet stone the swarm-song surges up through the stairwell to meet her, coiling around her name like a hook sinking into flesh — she can still feel it there now, cold and humming just beneath her skin, even as she straightens and does not stop. Anselm catches something in that surge too: beneath the wordless drone, for half a heartbeat, a boy's voice, thin and afraid. Yarrow holds the boat steady against the current as Ilse straightens, defeated, murmuring half a prayer to a Saint who hasn't answered in eleven years. The spiral stair up into the belltower stands open before you now, dark and dripping, the song pulling harder with every step closer.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Black water gives way to a narrow stone stair spiraling up into the temple's bones, the swarm-song growing louder with every step until it feels less like sound and more like pressure behind the eyes. Halfway up, the stairwell opens onto a landing where two pilgrims kneel in the wet dark, swaying, humming along with the tower above — their eyes turn toward the lantern light and the newcomers all at once. Above them, through a gap in the rotted floor, you can just glimpse a small bare foot dangling motionless over the edge of the bell-loft. The stone here answers every footstep with an echo, and the song seems to answer back.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I can hear where it breaks. There's a moment between every note where the song stops holding them so tight.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra plants her feet on the wet stone and closes her eyes, shutting out everything but the sound. The swarm-song hums through the pilgrims' swaying bodies—not random, not chaos, but a pattern. A breath in, a breath out. And in that space between, where the call falters for just a moment, she sees it: the gap where she can move.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The song has them pinned. I can pass through.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps forward with quiet certainty, his lips moving in words of warding as his fingers trace patterns through the stale air—weaving his knowledge of the hive's hunger into a narrow path between the song's coils, moving past the swaying pilgrims toward the stairs above.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I didn't come all this way to leave him to them.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock locks eyes on the dangling foot above and drives forward through the lantern-light, her powerful frame cutting through the swaying pilgrims without hesitation, determined not to let anything — not the song, not them, not herself — stop her from reaching Tomas.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I'm sorry for this. The boy comes down from that tower with us.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow doesn't hesitate. He advances with the sharp, economical movements of a trained militia guard—reading the rhythm of their swaying, the reach of their grasping hands. The nearest pilgrim lurches forward with the song pulling at them, and Yarrow meets the movement head-on, using discipline and hard-won technique to neutralize the threat without more cruelty than necessary. These people are victims of the blight; that doesn't make them less dangerous to the boy above.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: No—no, I hear it, I *have* it, I know where—

transcript.text: Petra accepts a compel.

transcript.text: Yarrow drives the pilgrim back and pins him against the wet stone, but the man's flailing arm rakes a rusted nail across Yarrow's forearm before he goes still — a shallow scratch, but an open wound all the same, right where the hive blight likes to find purchase.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's stillness breaks the spell just enough — for one heartbeat the whole landing seems to hold its breath in the gap between notes, and in that gap the others move. Anselm slides through the swaying pilgrims like smoke through a keyhole, his warding-words never faltering, and reaches the base of the stairs untouched. Caddock shoulders past a groping hand without slowing, prayer-knots still wound tight around her wrist, her eyes never leaving that small dangling foot above. Yarrow's pilgrim goes down hard under a textbook grapple — but as the man thrashes, a rusted nail buried in his ragged sleeve catches Yarrow's forearm, opening a shallow line of blood right where the hive loves to take root. The swarm-song shivers, as if it felt that wound open, and reaches for Petra's name again — she staggers but holds, teeth gritted, the gap in the pattern still hers to read. Above, through the rotted floor, the small foot doesn't move. The stairs to the belltower stand open now — but the song is still climbing toward a crescendo, and Yarrow's arm is already starting to itch.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I've got the gap. I won't let it take him.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra drives up the stone stairs into the darkness, her entire focus narrowing to that precious gap in the swarm-song's pattern. The song shrieks her name, surging and swelling around her, but she's found its rhythm—the break between every note where its hooks falter—and she follows that thread upward like a lifeline, invoking the gap she's already claimed to shield her climb.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm climbs the spiral stairs with quiet determination, his warding-words rising against the crescendoing song, fingers still weaving patterns of protection as he pushes toward the bell-loft.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I'm coming for you, Tomas.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock charges up the winding stairs toward the bell-loft, prayer-knots wound tight around her wrist, her powerful frame driving upward through the mounting pressure of the swarm-song—her jaw set, her eyes fixed on Tomas's dangling foot above, refusing to slow or stop.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I know what this is. It won't take hold of me. Not yet. Keep moving—Tomas comes down from that tower with us.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow feels the itch bloom and spread under his skin where the nail caught him—the hive blight taking root in blood like seeds in soil. For one sickening moment the swarm-song wraps around his thoughts like fingers tightening, pulling him toward that swaying, humming darkness. He's seen what it does. He's *come* to save a boy from exactly this. He clamps his teeth together hard, presses his bleeding forearm against his ribs, and doesn't hesitate—doesn't give the song even a moment of purchase. Each step up the spiral stairs is a small violence of refusal, his breath controlled and sharp, his eyes on the darkness above where the small foot dangled motionless. The infection can wait. The boy cannot.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: No—no, I *know* what I'm doing, I can still— Keep going, all of you, I'm right behind you—

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text:
All four of you burst into the belltower together, and for a moment the swarm-song simply stops — cut off mid-note, as if the tower itself flinched. Petra's stolen rhythm carries her straight to the gap in the floor; Anselm's wards flare cold and silver around the doorway, holding the song's coils at bay; Caddock doesn't slow, doesn't think, just crosses the rotten boards and gets both arms under Tomas's small body before the boy can slip further over the edge. He's limp, breathing, eyes half-open and unseeing — hive-touched but not yet lost, not yet feral. Yarrow reaches the top last, forearm throbbing, and plants himself in the doorway like a wall between the pilgrims below and the boy above. The great bell hangs silent and rusted overhead, and for the first time in three nights, nothing answers it.

But the itch in Yarrow's arm is spreading — a faint warmth under the skin that has nothing to do with the climb — and somewhere below, the pilgrims are beginning to stir again, remembering their feet.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The belltower is open to the grey sky, rain sheeting through gaps where the roof rotted away years ago. The great bronze bell hangs silent and corroded, but lashed to its clapper with wet rope is a boy — Tomas, eyes glassy, lips moving in time with a hum that seems to rise from the water far below rather than from him. Coiled on the ledge beside the bell, watching you with the calm of a man already drowned, sits the Drowned Priest, his robes black with damp, a rusted knife loose in one hand — not raised, not yet. "You hear it too, don't you," he says, looking at Petra. "It only sings to the ones it already loves."

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The song may have its hooks in me, but my vow goes deeper than any swarm-song—you're not making Tomas into another puppet.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra rushes toward the Drowned Priest with sudden speed, using her momentum to either disarm him or drive him back from the bell, buying herself space to reach Tomas and work at the rope binding him.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: He's not yours.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps forward with quick, economical motion, moving to position himself squarely at Tomas's side—a physical barrier between the knife and the boy, solid and immovable. His warding-words tighten, sharpening from protection into the keener cadence of exorcism.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I've delivered babies in a hundred storms, priest. A rusted knife won't stop me from helping a child.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock strides forward without hesitation toward Tomas, her jaw set and her eyes fixed on the bell. She moves with the steady purpose of a woman who's weathered far worse—not fast, not reckless, just inevitable.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Step away from the boy.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow advances on the Drowned Priest in quick, purposeful strides, closing the distance. The scratch on his forearm burns, but he pushes through it—this is what he trained for, what he *failed* at once before and won't fail at again. The boy sways above the black water, and between them stands a calm man with a rusted knife. Yarrow's body knows what to do: he will hold this line.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's rush connects — she slams into the Drowned Priest and drives him back a step from the bell — but her boot skids on the rain-slick ledge and she has to grab the corroded bell-frame to stop herself pitching toward the gap in the floor, the swarm-song surging louder in her skull the instant her hand touches old bronze.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text:
Petra's shoulder-check sends the Drowned Priest stumbling back against the bell's rim, knife arm flung wide — but her grab for the frame closes her fist around cold, weeping bronze, and the swarm-song floods up through the metal into her bones. For one terrible breath her name isn't a name anymore, just a note in the tower's endless hum, and her feet root to the ledge as if the bell itself has claimed her.

Anselm doesn't wait to see how it resolves. He plants himself at Tomas's side like a stone dropped into the flood, his warding-words snapping from a shield into something sharper — an exorcist's cadence that makes the wet rope hiss and the boy's glassy eyes flicker, just once, toward something like recognition. Caddock arrives a heartbeat later, steady as a midwife who's never once let a storm dictate the hour, and her fingers are already working the sodden knots at Tomas's wrists.

Yarrow closes the last of the distance and lands a solid blow across the priest's ribs — the man grunts, more surprised than hurt, robes darkening where the strike caught him — but even reeling, he doesn't drop the knife. His eyes flick past Yarrow to Petra, frozen and glassy-eyed with her hand fused to the bell, and something like satisfaction crosses his drowned face. "There," he breathes. "She hears it now. Let her ring it herself."

Tomas's ropes are half-cut, the boy stirring, but the priest is still standing, still armed, and Petra is caught fast in the swarm-song's grip with her hand on the one thing in the tower that can call it louder.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The song may have called my name, but it's not my master. This bell knows me, knows my hand. And I'm not ringing it for you.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's feet root deeper into the ledge with each pulse of the swarm-song, her hand welded to cold bronze—but her apprenticeship runs deeper than the song's reach. She draws a harsh breath and rings the bell with the precision of a hand that's known that rope since childhood, pulling a note that cuts clean through the drowning drone. For one crystalline moment the song stumbles, shattered by bronze and certainty, and the ice in her veins cracks enough to move.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm's warding-words sharpen and pivot from Tomas toward Petra, his exorcist cadence cutting against the swarm-song's grip on the corroded bell, working to break the hold before it drags her under.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: You're free, Tomas. I've got you now.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock finishes the last knot and tears the rope free. She grabs Tomas firmly around the waist and hauls him down from the bell's clapper, moving with the steady purpose of a woman who's never let chaos dictate her work.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Step back from the bell.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow drives forward without hesitation, pressing the Drowned Priest with the relentless focus of someone drilled into holding a line. His weight stays low and centered, ready to absorb whatever comes back at him and keep advancing. His eyes never leave the knife—tracking the priest's posture, the set of his shoulders, the angle of that rusted blade. There's no room for the priest to regroup, no space to turn his satisfaction into action. Yarrow will not yield this ground.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's own ring shatters the bell's grip on her — the swarm-song recoils like a burned hand, and her fingers finally peel free of the corroded bronze, breath ragged but her own again. Anselm's exorcist cadence catches the last threads of the song as they try to snap back around her, unraveling them into nothing before they can take hold twice. Behind them, Caddock already has Tomas clear of the gap, the boy blinking rain-wet and dazed but present — present, and hers, not the tower's. The Drowned Priest reels under Yarrow's second blow, robes torn, ribs surely cracked, but he plants his feet against the ledge's edge and slashes back with the last of his strength, the rusted knife hissing through empty air where Yarrow no longer stands — Yarrow reads the arc and simply isn't there when it lands, and now the priest has nowhere left to retreat but the black water below.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The bell answers to me, not you.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps forward with sudden certainty, the song's chains shattered, and strikes at the priest with focused precision—driving him back toward the rain-slick ledge's edge.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: You're finished here, priest. Step back or fall—those are your only choices now.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock strides forward without hesitation and plants herself at Yarrow's side. She drives her shoulder into the priest's ribs with all the relentless weight she brings to pulling children through difficult births—not reckless, just inevitable. The priest staggers backward, boots scraping the wet ledge at the very edge.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: You're done here, priest. Drop the blade.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow closes in with the same relentless forward drive he's shown all round, eyes locked on the knife, weight centered and ready to see this through. There's nowhere left for the priest to go but the black water, and Yarrow won't let him retreat anywhere else.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's strike lands true, driving the priest back — but her own momentum carries her past him, boots skidding off the ledge's rotten edge. She pitches toward the black water below and only just catches a jut of broken stone with her fingertips, dangling half over the drop, the swarm-song hissing up at her from beneath the surface. Consequence: MILD — Winded and Off-Balance.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Caddock's shoulder drives into the priest's cracked ribs with all the inevitability of a hard labor finally ending, and Yarrow's follow-through leaves nowhere left to stand — the Drowned Priest teeters on the rotten ledge, robes tearing, and then the black water takes him, swallowing his last words along with the rest of him. The swarm-song shudders, stutters, and goes quiet, as if the tower itself has lost its voice. Petra hangs half over the drop, fingertips white on broken stone, winded and off-balance — but Anselm is already there, hauling her back onto the ledge by the wrist, the exorcist's wards flickering out now that the priest is gone. Tomas sags against Caddock, blinking rain from his lashes, present in his own eyes for the first time since they arrived. Below, the belltower's silence spreads outward across the flooded nave like a held breath finally released — the hive's hold on this place, at least, is broken.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The Drowned Priest is gone, swallowed by the black water below, but his last shriek hasn't faded — it's caught in the bell, echoing wrong, and Tomas still hangs lashed to the clapper, lips moving in time with a hum that no longer has a singer. The rain sheets down through the broken roof, and the bronze bell begins, very softly, to sway on its own. Below, the water churns once, twice — something down there hasn't finished with you yet. Petra can feel the note trying to find her name again; Tomas's ropes are wet, swollen, cinched tight around a boy too pain-blind to help you save him.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Hold on, Tomas—I've got you.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra moves to Tomas without hesitation and tears at the ropes binding him to the clapper. The rope is swollen with floodwater and brutally knotted, but her fingers work with the strength and speed of someone raised around bell-line, pulling and twisting, racing against the bell's unnatural sway.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Not here. Not this child.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm's warding cadence transforms into a direct assault, his words of power building to a crescendo of cold silver as he directs them at the churning presence in the water below, driving the swarm-song back and attempting to sever its grip on the bell tower and on Tomas both.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I've brought children into this world in worse weather than this, boy - you think I can't get you free?

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock reaches the bell clapper without hesitation, her scarred hands already working at the wet ropes binding Tomas, treating them like she would untangle a birth cord - methodical, practiced, no wasted motion. Rain streams down her face and she doesn't blink.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I've got you!

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow drops low at the ledge's edge, boots planted hard against the slick wet stone, extending his arm down toward Petra with all his weight braced to pull her clear of the water and the song.)

transcript.text: Petra tears the ropes free of Tomas's wrists at last, but the wet knot she rips loose whips back and cracks across her knuckles hard enough to split skin — a stinging, open wound, right where the hive blight loves to find purchase.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Anselm's silver cadence slams into the thing churning below and it recoils, its grip on the bell and the boy broken — but the effort claws something back out of him, tearing loose the memory of his sister's last cry so vividly he staggers, momentarily deaf to everything but her voice, and doesn't hear the bell's dying groan overhead.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Yarrow's arm closes around Petra's wrist and he hauls her up and clear of the black water — but the wrenching pull tears something in his shoulder, and his arm goes half-numb and useless at his side, hanging like dead weight even as he grits through it.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Tomas drops free into Caddock's arms the instant the last knot gives, gasping, blinking rain out of glassy eyes that are — slowly — starting to look like a nine-year-old's again instead of the swarm's. Overhead the great bell shudders on its corroded mount, groaning through one last dying note before it goes still and silent for the first time in years. Below, the water goes flat and quiet, the churning presence Anselm scourged with silver light sinking back into the dark, wounded and sullen rather than gone. Yarrow's arm hangs useless at his side, teeth gritted against the pain, but he doesn't let go of Petra's wrist until she's fully clear of the ledge. Anselm sways where he stands, his sister's cry still ringing in his skull louder than any warding-word, deaf for a long moment to the rain, the boy's ragged breathing, everything but that old drowned voice. Petra's knuckles split and bleeding where the rope whipped back — a small wound, but an open one, right where the hive likes to find purchase. For now, though, the belltower holds four exhausted rescuers, one shaking boy wrapped in Caddock's coat, and a silence that finally feels like theirs.
